Q112785721.summary: In the small apse of a Thessaloniki church, a young, beardless Christ sits on a rainbow within a luminous circle of glory, holding an open scroll of praise and surrounded by the four living creatures, while two prophets gaze up at him in awe from the banks of the rivers of Paradise. It is a vision of the Lord's appearing, drawn from Ezekiel and the Book of Revelation, and among the finest early Byzantine mosaics to survive. An inscription below the scene speaks of the church as a life-giving spring that receives and nourishes the souls of the faithful.
facts: A Byzantine legend says the mosaic was hidden under an ox-hide and mortar to protect it from iconoclasts, and later miraculously revealed; it was rediscovered in the early 20th century beneath Ottoman-era plaster.

The church served as a mosque during the Ottoman period and was reconsecrated as an Orthodox church in 1921, when it came to be called after Saint David the Dendrite; its original dedication is uncertain, perhaps to Christ the Saviour.
The two prophets are usually identified as Ezekiel and Habakkuk (some propose Isaiah), who recorded visions of God's glory.
Since 1988 the church has formed part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Paleochristian and Byzantine Monuments of Thessaloniki'.
Q112785721.notes: The identity of the two witnesses is debated (Ezekiel and Habakkuk is the most widely held view; Grabar proposed Peter and Paul).

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-107-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits in a mandorla borne by four angels and flanked by four more, holding a scroll and raising his hand in speech: 'be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens'. To the left, rays of the sun fall on the psalmist, who walks before a tabernacle carrying a harp, a lute and a measuring rod, ready to 'awake the dawn'. Below, armies besiege a walled city.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-107-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-san-widows-mite.summary: At the left a veiled widow drops her coins into the temple treasury, shown as a small table; at the centre Christ, haloed and in purple, raises his hand to point out her gift to the disciple who stands beside him. The quiet scene illustrates Christ's teaching that the poor widow 'cast in more than they all'.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

cur:monumental-thessaloniki-hagia-sophia.summary: In the centre of the dome, Christ sits on a rainbow within a circle of light, raising his right hand in blessing, as two angels in flight bear the glory upward. Around the drum below (not shown here) stand the Virgin, two angels and the twelve apostles among trees. The inscription ringing the scene quotes the angels' words at the Ascension.
facts: The dome inscription quotes Acts 1:11: 'Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?'
The church, built in the 7th century on the model of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, is part of the UNESCO site of the Paleochristian and Byzantine Monuments of Thessalonika.
Much of the interior was plastered over after the Great Fire of 1917, and the dome was not restored until 1980.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Saint Sophia Church, Thessaloniki - Dome mosaic
UNESCO: Paleochristian and Byzantine Monuments of Thessalonika

cur:monumental-thessaloniki-hagia-sophia.notes: The date is usually given as the 880s on the basis of the dome's inscriptions; exact dating is debated.

europeana:9200579/eegz3kjq.summary: On this small devotional card Christ stands barefoot on soft clouds in a long white robe and mantle, his right hand open towards the viewer and his left pointing to the flaming heart shown on his breast. The caption reads 'Sacro Cuore di Gesù'. Wellcome identifies the figure as Christ in the form in which he appeared to St Margaret Mary Alacoque, the visionary behind the modern devotion to the Sacred Heart.
facts: The modern devotion to the Sacred Heart derives from the visions reported by the French nun Margaret Mary Alacoque between 1673 and 1675.
The card is tiny, about 10.8 × 5.8 cm, with decoratively shaped edges typical of early 20th-century holy cards (Wellcome Collection 31493i).
europeana:9200579/eegz3kjq.notes: Wellcome dates it '[between 1910 and 1919]'; our '191X'/year 191 was a parsing error. Place inferred from the Italian caption. The Wellcome record has been merged into work x234febn.

Q116256182.summary: In this small ivory icon, Christ Pantokrator, 'Ruler of All', appears half-length and frontal, his bearded face framed by a cross-nimbus and long hair, blessing with his right hand and holding a jewelled Gospel book in his left. The carving is crisp and severe, concentrating all attention on the steady gaze. It distils the image that dominated the domes and apses of Byzantine churches into an object small enough to hold.
facts: The Met defines the Pantokrator type as a frontal, half-length bearded Christ holding a Gospel book and blessing.
It came to the Met from the collection of Georges Hoentschel through J. Pierpont Morgan (gift of 1917) and was shown in the 2013 exhibition on Hoentschel at the Bard Graduate Center.
